name: Lacquer & Nerve
description:
Released in 2208 exclusively through licensed neural feed distributors, 'Lacquer & Nerve' is the debut full-length from Ossian Collective, a five-person ensemble based out of a converted warehouse studio in Tier 3 who spent four years building the album's architecture around the specific perceptual characteristics of mid-range BCI augmentation. The album was designed in three simultaneous layers: a conventional audio mix accessible to unaugmented listeners, a secondary harmonic layer audible only to chrome-enhanced hearing, and a tertiary neural texture — not sound exactly, but sensation — delivered through BCI neural feed that produces something between temperature change and color impression. Listeners without augmentation report it as a clean, melancholic ambient record. Listeners with full neural sync describe an experience that has no vocabulary yet.

The standout track 'Periosteum' builds over fourteen minutes from near-silence into a dense lattice of South American koto-adjacent strings, sub-bass frequencies below normal human hearing, and — for augmented listeners — a wash of what many describe as 'the feeling of remembering something you never experienced.' 'Copper Transit' is a rare upbeat moment, structured around an Afro-Brazilian clave pattern rendered in synthetic metallics, which in neural-feed mode apparently triggers mild proprioceptive displacement. The closing piece, 'What the Chrome Hears,' is eight minutes of nothing audible at all — it exists only as a neural texture, and it became a minor controversy when augmented listeners began describing shared imagery.
creator: Ossian Collective
audience: Tier 3 and Tier 4 professionals with mid-to-high grade BCI augmentation, augmentation subculture enthusiasts, ambient music critics
cultural_impact: The album sparked a significant debate in Meridian 88's augmentation-rights community about whether music designed for augmented perception constitutes a form of discrimination against the unaugmented poor — BCI upgrades capable of full neural-feed reception cost between Φ8,000 and Φ40,000, placing the full album experience far outside Tier 1 and Tier 2 reach. Ossian Collective released a statement defending tiered listening as 'honest about its context,' which satisfied no one. Despite the controversy — or because of it — the album sold extremely well in Tier 3 and Tier 4, and the shared-imagery phenomenon reported by listeners of 'What the Chrome Hears' has been cited in three separate neurological research papers.
story_hooks: Several listeners of 'What the Chrome Hears' report experiencing identical imagery — a specific corridor, a specific face — and someone is quietly collecting their testimonies.

A Tier 1 hardware hacker claims to have cracked the neural-feed layer and is distributing a bootleg version playable on black-market BCI implants; Vantablack's enforcement division wants the source code suppressed.

A character with a malfunctioning BCI experiences the album's neural layer unexpectedly and involuntarily during a critical moment — and what they perceive changes their understanding of something they thought they knew.
